en: "The Upaniṣadic statement, 'That Brahman is indeed one without a second,' surely negates the existence of anything other than Brahman. (YS 1)
To this we reply: regarding the expression "non-dual" (*advitīya*), what compound is intended?
Is it a *tatpuruṣa* or, rather, a *bahuvrīhi*? Let it be stated. (YS 2)

In the former [type of comparison], the subsequent term is primarily intended to express the referent of the word; in that case, Brahman is either something other than that or something similar to it. (YS 3)
Alternatively, it may be contradictory to that; yet among these three, nothing else subverts [the first].
Whether there is difference or similarity, the second [alternative] is certainly established. (YS 4)
Because, in the case of contradiction, the third [position] is contradicted by the second, or the first by the second, Brahman is thereby attained. (YS 5)

Therefore, all the groups of meanings beginning with the third case, together with the first, remain uncontradicted in their own respective senses once they have been touched by the second case in that manner. (YS 6)
Now, is it not the case that the negative particle (nañ) negates everything other than Brahman? For the mention of "the second" is an indicator (upalakṣaṇa) of everything [other than Brahman]. (YS 7)
The negation is not of this kind, for from it nothing second is understood—neither something other than that, nor its opposite, nor anything similar to it. (YS 8)
If it is intended that Brahman is that which does not possess a second at all, then the descriptions of its characteristics as "truth" and so forth would become non-characteristics. (YS 9)

In the case of "non-dual" (*advitīya*), since the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) has its own inherent referent—the mere absence of a second object—there would be no syntactic connection with the word "Brahman. (YSsi 10)
In that case, the second emptiness is not a qualification of Brahman;
or, if it were a qualification, that Brahman would be either a third or a first [Brahman]. (YS 1.11)
Everything as previously mentioned applies to the bahuvrīhi compound;
those who are the first among the Brahmins and those who are the third and so forth in the three worlds [are included]. (YSi 12)
Because Brahman is non-dual, those who abide in themselves remain unassailed;
furthermore, this is so when the compound is understood as a bahuvrīhi. (YS 1.3)
The meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), which functions as a modifier, does not enter into a syntactic relation with another word-meaning;
for only when there is a connection with another meaning is the use of the genitive case in the phrase "of which" (*yasya*) appropriate.
The non-existence of a second entity is neither Brahman nor a qualifier;
for that which is non-existent cannot be Brahman, nor can it be a qualifier. (YSi 15)
Therefore, the existence of phenomenal diversity is not sublated by the scriptures on non-duality;
it is established by the force of its own means of valid cognition and is even approved by scripture.
Therefore, this meaning of the Vedic scripture "Brahman is without a second" is stated:
there has been, is, and will be nothing capable of being counted as a second.
Whether equal or superior to him, that which is multiplied as his second [aspect] is such that this world is but a mere fraction of his array of manifestations (*vibhava-vyūha*). (YS 18)
How could it become the object of a second speech? Just as [one says]: "The King of Cola is the sole emperor on earth today. (YSi 19)
Thus, these words are intended to prevent one from becoming a king equal to him, but they do not prohibit [the taking of] his servants, sons, wives, and so forth. (YSi 20)
Likewise, there are millions of Brahmā-eggs containing gods, asuras, and humans,
yet [the Lord] remains untouched by afflictions, karma, their maturation, and so forth, for He is the Sovereign of all.
These [powers] are but drops and sprays from the ocean of the majesty and glory of Viṣṇu, who is a treasury of the sixfold qualities beginning with knowledge and whose power is inconceivable.
Who indeed, counting the seven oceans by snapping their fingers, could count the waves, foam, bubbles, and droplets? (YS 23)
Just as when it is said, "There is only one sun in the vault of the sky, not a second," by this statement the rays of the sun are not thereby negated; so it is here. (YSŚ 24)

Just as a number that is itself to be counted is not counted within the enumeration of the primary objects to be counted, because it exists separately there, like any other object to be counted. (YS 25)
Likewise,
by stating, "One foot of this is all beings; its three feet are the immortal in heaven," [the Veda] established the entire world as being of such a nature.
Thus, such is his greatness; yet he is indeed greater than that.
Where one knows nothing else—that is the Bhūman, the limit, the interval.
"Manifest fear arises for him," and so forth—such are the supreme scriptural passages. (Yogasūtrabhāṣya 1.27)
"For whom this entire universe and world is like a minute atom compared to Mount Meru"—such [statements] refer to the fact that the whole exists in such a manner for Him. (YS 28)
The entire world, both stationary and moving, consisting of all modifications, is merely a matter of verbal designation;
only the immutable root cause is real. (YS 2.29)
The effect is non-different from the cause, like sparks from a fire, as demonstrated by a wide variety of examples such as clay, iron, and seeds. (YSiS 30)
The fire was unable to burn the grass that had been consumed by it, nor was the wind able to move it, because it had entered into it through its own power. (YS 31)
"By the cognition of a single primary [principle], everything becomes known"—by such Vedic statements and by the authoritative scriptures rooted therein as well. (YSŚi 32)
"This phenomenal world, composed of both consciousness and the unconscious, attains its existence through Brahman as its self"—thus is the glory of Brahman established, and it is not denied. (YS 33)
If that [duality] were denied in its entirety because it is false in both worldly and Vedic contexts,
then worldly transactions would perish, and likewise, even the cognition of Brahman would cease to exist.
"Even though [perception and so forth] are false, there is no contradiction because they possess conventional truth;
this view regarding perception and the rest was already thoroughly refuted previously. (YSsi 35)

Therefore, it is established that the world is not sublated by the cognition of the non-duality of Brahman arising from the Upaniṣads, because the world is a manifestation (vibhūti) of Brahman. (YS 36)
If it exists, how can there be the cognition that "the proliferation does not exist"?
Or if it does not exist, how could there be the cognition that "it exists" with respect to it? (YS 37)
Likewise, the simultaneous existence and non-existence of a single thing is impossible due to contradiction;
for when two contradictory pairs meet, they result in the cognition of both existence and non-existence. (YS 38)
Because there is no certainty regarding the object of either of those two,
the Jains, however, have maintained that the manifold world (prapañca) is both existent and non-existent.

Placing the attainment of existence at the forefront, the Sāṅkhyas, however, maintain that because the cognition "it does not exist" arises, existence is always present within the proliferation of conceptual construction (prapañca). (YS 40)
In the face of the perilous conflict of the two contradictory positions— existence and non-existence— as they are encountered through their respective conditions,

some have declared that the manifold world (*prapañca*) is "inexpressible" (*anirvācya*) in terms of being both existent and non-existent, by way of negating the aspects of existence and non-existence in order to resolve the contradiction. (YSi 41)
Others have proclaimed a systematic distinction, thinking that the existence or non-existence of jars and the like is determined by the differentiation of place, time, and so forth. (YS 42)
Thus, when doubt has arisen due to the clash of disputants,
a definitive resolution is made therein according to the Mīmāṃsaka doctrine.
If non-existence were perceived within the very nature of the jar, then existence and non-existence would indeed coexist simultaneously in jars and other such things. (YS 44)

For this reason, due to the differences in place, time, and state, our cognitions arise as "it exists" or "it does not exist" with respect to the thought: "Now this is here; it is not there. (YS 4.45)

Therefore, existence and non-existence regarding jars and other things are established through distinctions such as place; since that [opposing] argument has been refuted here, its occurrence is impossible.
Indeed, connection with space and so forth is possible only for that which exists;
it is not accepted that non-existence becomes existence through connection with space and time. (YS 47)
A relation depends on two relata; therefore, that which exists would always exist.
For that which does not exist to attain existence through the activity of causal factors at the moment of birth is an extreme impossibility.
Therefore, the phenomenal world (prapañca), which has a beginning and an end, is included within the category of existence;
and it has been said:
"That which does not exist at the beginning and at the end likewise does not exist in the middle."

Therefore, that whose existence is certain should be accepted as being always existent. (YS 49) Thus, for that which is non-existent, there is always non-existence because it lacks connection with production, like a sky-flower.
In this world, there is no distinction between what is non-existent previously and what is absolutely non-existent. (YS 50)

Since the statement "That thou art" was heard even with reference to Śvetaketu in the sixth chapter [of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad], how could there be the possibility of its primary meaning [being established] there?

The conscious self denoted by the term *tvaṃ* (you), afflicted by miserliness, grief, and suffering, is [in reality] the referent of the term *tat* (that)—the omniscient one whose volitions are true and who is an ocean of boundless bliss.
How can the unity of these two be like light and darkness? (YSi 52)

Whether the qualifying attribute (guṇa) resides in the referent of "you" (tvam), or is external to it, or resides in the referent of "that" (tat)—in any case, the identity of meaning between the words "that" (tat) and "thou" (tvam) is ruled out from afar. (YSi 53)
Whether the attributes such as ignorance and omniscience, suffering and happiness, and so forth,
serve as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) or as mere indicators (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the element of consciousness (*cid-dhātu*),
a distinction would arise between the two meanings [of "you" and "that"] due to the transfer of contradictory qualities. (YS 54)

To claim that the two words "That" (tat) and "Thou" (tvam) refer to a single individual consciousness by means of discarding a portion of their denotable meaning—just as in the case of "This is that cow"—is untenable. (YSsi 55)
Due to differences in place, time, and state, even with respect to a single substratum,
because of the transition into contradictory pairs of opposites, it is appropriate to say, "This is that cow."
In the case of the self-luminous element of consciousness, when it encounters contradictory pairs of opposites,
there is no determining factor whatsoever— such as place, time, or state.
In the self-luminous conscious Self, from which all dualities have been shaken off, scripture would become devoid of an object, because the delusion of the evil of duality no longer exists. (YS 58)

By this [same principle], qualities such as having true desires and being the cause of the world are superimposed upon the Supreme [Self] through the limiting adjunct of Māyā; whereas sorrow, delusion, and the like are superimposed [upon it] through the limiting adjunct of Avidyā. (YSi 59)

Regarding the view that there is no destruction for the *jīva* when it has ignorance as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), this is the opinion of those who know only the minor Brahman; it has already been refuted previously. (YS 60)

Regarding the nature of consciousness, whether it be the pure essence or that which is qualified, there are limiting adjuncts such as *māyā* and *avidyā*. In the former case, there would be total confusion due to the lack of distinction between the Supreme and the individual soul (*jīva*).

In the latter case as well, if consciousness, though qualified, is likewise [the same], then—since the nature of consciousness is indeed without division—it is merely through the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of *māyā*, *avidyā*, and so forth, that it appears as if divided and deluded; thus it is considered "qualified" by you. (YSsi_62)
Do phenomena situated as mere bystanders not touch their own essential nature?
Indeed, Devadatta is not left unhurt by the severing of the head of the man with the staff. (YS 63)
Furthermore, the claim that the meaning of such passages as "That thou art" consists in the exclusion of the non-conscious portion so that only consciousness remains is also untenable. (YSsi 64)
When the state of being non-Brahman and non-self is negated, pure consciousness remains as the direct witness.
The two terms *tat* and *tvam* have as their object the identity between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*).
That identity, in its primary sense of function, likewise rests upon two distinct entities. (YS Si 65)
But as for the dilemma regarding difference and non-difference that you have raised,
it is pointless, since bondage— whether consisting of the bound or the binding— is unreal due to their lack of distinction.
Non-difference, however, is that which sublates difference between two things that serve as its own substrata;
difference is the mutual non-identity of entities—such is the nature of these two.
Having accepted the very nature [of things], you subject it to the dilemmas of difference and non-difference;
therefore, by that contradiction, you are defeated by the refutation of your own words.

The conceptualization of the relationship between difference and non-difference, and of existence and non-existence, is entirely beyond the scope of direct perception; it is nothing but a parching of the throat.
Just as the cognition of "blue" regarding a blue lotus is indeed the cognition of "blue," so too does this very blue lotus manifest directly to us as "this is a blue lotus. (YSi 70)

Just as, even when the connection and relation are known and within the range of the senses, there occurs the delusion of superimposing fallacious conceptual constructions such as difference and non-difference; [so it is with the Self]. (YS 71)

In the same way, when the relationship of identity is rooted in scripture and direct perception, the delusion of false reasoning and conceptual construction is warded off by the staff of scripture. (YS Si 72)
And the flawless, non-human scripture, out of extreme reverence, repeatedly declares that "That" is the reality, [thereby teaching] the identity between Brahman and the individual soul. (YS 73)

The liberated self, situated within the lake of the bliss of Brahman, thrives in happiness. Furthermore, because the possessor of the fruit is absent when the fruit [is realized], liberation would not be a human goal; for if only the element of consciousness remains, for whom would liberation be the fruit? (YS 74)
Furthermore, what kind of consciousness manifests in the form of conceptual proliferation?
It is certainly not the cognition of a jar, because that [cognition] is observed even when it does not exist. (YSsi 75)
For it cannot be said that when that [consciousness] is unarisen or destroyed, the entire world does not exist,
because that would contradict what has been stated and direct perception;
nor is there another consciousness [that perceives it], because even upon its destruction, other things are still perceived.
Indeed, consciousness is one and non-different; no cognition of difference exists within it.
For while jars and other objects are differentiated, that consciousness is not, because it is self-luminous.
If it is argued that the cognition of a jar does not manifest at the time of the perception of a cloth, this is not so;
for while the jar indeed does not manifest, that [cognition] itself clearly shines forth.

If it is argued that the cognition excluded from the jar does not manifest, then by the word "exclusion" (vyāvṛtti) is that very same [cognition] expressed, or something else? If it is that very same [cognition], then it manifests; if it is something else, do not speak of its manifestation. (YSsi 79)

Furthermore, since this [consciousness] is self-luminous and formless, there can be no delusion regarding the apprehension of multiplicity from its own side, except through the diversity of objects. (YS 80)
Neither the entity nor its property is non-perceptual or non-worldly;
even the distinction between objects such as jars and so forth is merely characterized by delusion.
When that is so, then from that [cause] arises the emergence of the discernment of distinctions through the intellect;
how much less, then, could there be for it any connection with ultimate reality?
Furthermore, for that which is self-luminous, the establishment of its prior non-existence and so forth would have to occur either by itself or through another;
however, it is not tenable that this occurs by itself. (YSsi 83)
Because its absence would be impossible while it itself exists due to contradiction, and because self-luminosity—which is its own cause—is impossible even when it is absent;
and because consciousness has no other object, it cannot be known from another either. (YS 84)

Furthermore, it is impossible for the distinctions and so forth of the object of cognition to be attributes of consciousness, just like color and other such qualities; therefore, consciousness is non-dual and self-luminous.
Therefore, the learned knowers of Brahman understand that whatever has been prattled regarding its distinctions, such as "dissimilar" and so forth, is merely the play of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Ah! This instruction on Brahman shines for those who possess faith;
we, however, are lacking in faith, and thus we seek logical reasoning.
For cognitions manifest directly as distinct from one another for each individual subject, just like pleasure, pain, and so forth. (YS 88)
For us, the distinction between conjunction, desire, and so forth—which is manifested through their relations—is not non-existent in itself, nor is it imperceptible. (YS 89)
If consciousness alone is accepted as being omnipresent and eternal, then everything would always be manifest,
or else nothing at all would ever be manifest.
At that time, indeed, no fixed rule regarding the proximity or otherwise of the object of knowledge is possible, because consciousness,
like space, rests upon omnipresence.
Nor [is it established] by a difference in causes, because that is absent in the case of what is eternal;
nor by a plurality of essential natures, because its unity is maintained. (YS 4.12)
Consequently, it would follow that the deaf, the blind, and others could perceive sound and other objects;
furthermore, the distinction between teacher and disciple and so forth would result in being without any basis.

"Indeed, for us, there is nothing whatsoever called 'everything' that is distinct from consciousness; therefore, to urge [us] pointlessly that 'everything should always shine' is a baseless objection. (YSsi 94)
Tell me this, sir: why is it that blue and the like do not manifest? Or, if they do manifest, why is blue and the like not distinct from consciousness? (YS 95)
In the beginning, there is a stream of experience pleasant to the intellect, belonging to both worldly and Vedic discourse,
wherein neither words nor word-meanings appear as distinct entities.
In the second case, the intended non-duality of consciousness would be contradicted;
for if this manifold proliferation of diverse forms consists of consciousness, then since that consciousness is also of that same nature, it follows that it must be manifold. (YS Si 97)
Nor can it be argued that because it is a manifestation of ignorance, its distinction or non-distinction cannot be determined;
for when touched by the fire of logic, it behaves like an ornament made of lac.
For if this ignorance were held to consist in the mere absence of knowledge, then, because its nature would be indefinable, it could not determine anything at all. (YS 99)
If ignorance (*avidyā*) is something other than knowledge (*vidyā*), then it is well said that its distinction [from knowledge] is not established;

for the conceptual alternatives of whether it is different from or non-different from knowledge are not tenable. And to say that "this [ignorance] is something other than knowledge" is a poorly spoken word. 100.
Moreover, even if there were the existence of a different object for that [cognition], it would be imagined by delusion;
alas, if this were so, then ignorance itself would be knowledge from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Moreover, consciousness is pure and non-inert, whereas this ignorance is not like that;
for what reason, then, is it not determined to be something entirely distinct? (YS 1.102)
Moreover, this ignorance of yours, which consists of non-existence and so forth—is that knowledge (vidyā) consciousness, the object of knowledge, or perhaps the knower? (YS 103)
In its state of being an object of knowledge and in its state of being a knower, there is no cessation of these two for it [avidyā].
For ignorance does not cease through anything other than knowledge;
if you say it is consciousness itself, then surely its impossibility follows from your own position.
Furthermore, whether this [ignorance] is opposed to that [knowledge] or not, it can never exist anywhere,
because the entire world is pervaded by non-dual knowledge alone. (YS 105)
If you maintain that there is either a non-existence or something else contradictory to consciousness,
then at that time, abandon from afar your thesis of the non-duality of consciousness.
And to whom does this [bond] belong?
If it is said to belong to the *jīva*, and one asks who the *jīva* is to whom it belongs—surely, in this way, there would be an unresolved circularity (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*). (YS Si 107)
But ignorance cannot arise from the individual soul (jīva), nor can the individual soul exist without it;
for there is no equality between seed and sprout, since the production of a soul is logically impossible. (YSsi 108)
If Brahman is not omniscient, how does it wander about? For you,
there is no dependence on the notion of a self in the body produced by ignorance regarding the state of Brahman’s omniscience.
Because of the scriptural statement regarding its being of the nature of that [Self]. (YS 1.9)
If omniscience is false because it contains the appearance of differentiation, then why is it not true for that very same reason, like one's own words or other [cognitions]? (YS 110)
Just as the repetition of different words, numbers, and so forth are the differentiators of scriptural texts,
and just as they possess within them the manifestation of difference and are true to their meaning,
why should this [the teaching of the Self] not be likewise?
If ignorance were possible even in the omniscient one who is eternally liberated—just as darkness might exist within light—then it could not be removed by anyone. (YS 1.12)
"The authority of statements such as 'omniscience' is merely conventional;
however, the ultimate validity belongs to the words of non-duality. We see no restrictive principle for this other than your own insistence. (YSsi 113)
Since being the locus and being the counter-correlative are mutually contradictory,
how can Brahman, which is of a single essence, be understood as "existent"?
If Brahman is the substratum by virtue of its inwardness (*pratyaktva*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) by virtue of its nature as Brahman,

and if this distinction of forms produced [in Brahman] arises through the grace of ignorance (*avidyā*), then— since that ignorance too is dependent upon it— there is once again a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayaṇa*). (YS 1.15)
Since ignorance is not a real entity... (if this [critique] is not a characterization of its nature), then where have you observed this as a refutation of a real entity? (YS 116)
Because one's own thesis is prioritized, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
Since [the argument] is neither based on being a real entity (*vastutva*) nor on being a non-entity (*avastutva*), this is not a valid response. (YS 1.17)
Furthermore, if ignorance did not exist... how could there be a functional entity?
Nor is it accepted that it is like the non-existent sky-flower and such, which are treated as objects of conventional usage. (YS Si 118)
Nor does the statement "it is not a non-entity" necessarily establish its status as a real entity;
for if it is thought that the word "entity" is negated by the negative particle *nañ* taken as a whole, [that is not so]. (YSsi 119)

Whatever entity is first negated by the negative particle used in its entirety, that same entity is subsequently restored when the negative particle is used distributively; thus, it possesses the nature of a real thing.
Therefore, there is neither a real entity nor a non-entity, neither that which can be called existent nor that which is non-existent;
no distinction whatsoever shines forth— do not ever intend to speak thus.
Furthermore, tell me this: is this ignorance (*avidyā*), which is relied upon as the mother that brings about the maintenance of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*), one alone or many?
And likewise, is its locus—the transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*)—one or many? (YS 122)
If that [nature] were one, then it would have already been discarded by Śuka through his knowledge of Brahman; thus, your exertion for liberation is in vain. (YS 123)
It might be thought: "Vāmadeva, Śuka, and others do not exist for you at all;
since they have been dispelled by knowledge, the objection that 'ignorance exists now' is not raised. (YSsi 124)
For the distinction between the liberated and the unliberated, and so forth, is imagined through my own ignorance;
because it is an object of perception, it is like the manifold diversity of objects perceived in my own dream.

Furthermore, as for the statement that their liberation occurred through the knowledge of Brahman, that should be refuted by means of the reasoning applied to the account of liberation in a dream. // YSsi_126 //
But surely, how do you respond to another who establishes the manifold world (prapañca) as being imagined by their own ignorance through such an inference? (YS 1.127)

Whatever reason you intend to put forward for [the world] having ignorance as its cause would be the very same reason for that [ignorance] as well, just as in the case of the proof of an omniscient being.
Thus, since your doctrine is contradicted by mutually inconsistent statements, you appear as one who is merely prattling nonsense, as if saying, "There is a face. (YSi 129)

And just as the fear of liberation from that [dream] is similar to the expression of liberation within a dream, so it is for you as well; thus, your exertion for the sake of liberation is in vain. (YS Si 130)
Just as their liberation, though previously non-existent, is said to have become real through the knowledge of the Self, so too [is it] later through the knowledge of the Self.
Let it be declared that what is non-existent is false, yet appears as if existent; and you possess examples from dreams to support this statement.
Now, it is not undesirable for me that liberation will not occur, because since the self is eternally liberated, that [liberation] is already eternally established. (YS 1.33)
Thus, this [practice] would become a mounting of a vetāla at the beginning of rites for pacification and the like;
by which the labor of acquiring the knowledge of Brahman becomes all the more futile. (YSi 134)
Furthermore, although that [power] is eternally existent, because it is obstructed by ignorance, it is as if non-existent;
therefore, its manifestation is accepted as the fruit of knowledge. (YS 1.35)
Just as gold and other such items held in one's own hand are sought after when forgotten, and just as that very same object, once recognized as being in one's hand, brings peace; so it is here.

In the very same way, due to the non-recognition of the nature of the eternally established Self, the state of being a transmigrator is manifested; that state is [subsequently] revealed by the knowledge of Brahman. (YS 1.37)

Ah, what is this manifestation that is desired as the fruit of knowledge—a [manifestation] which resides in the very state of the essential nature of the self-luminous principle of consciousness? (YSŚ 138)
Is that consciousness itself, or am I? What is the nature of the thought "Brahman exists"?
If it is consciousness of one's own nature, then since that is eternal, it is not something newly produced.
Now, if the manifestation of the consciousness "I am Brahman" is intended [to be the result], then surely that is itself the knowledge of Brahman; how can it be its own fruit? (YS 1.40)

Furthermore, according to your view, that [knowledge] produced by sentences such as "That thou art" would be subject to origination and impermanent; consequently, fear would arise even for one who is liberated.
Moreover, those who understand conventional usage say that when an effect does not arise despite the presence of its full set of causes, that [absence] is called an "obstructer" (pratibandhaka).
In this case, what is that which has begun to arise from its own cause but does not reach completion because it is obstructed by ignorance? (YS 1.43)
There is no liberation because it is eternally established;
nor is there even the cognition "I am Brahman," for the consciousness "I am Brahman" lacks its full cause.
Since that [bond] exists for those in saṃsāra, how can it be obstructed?
Since that [effect] does not arise now due to the absence of its cause,
and not because it is obstructed, therefore that statement [of yours] is misplaced.

Moreover, the notion that "the individual soul (jīva) is one" is not tenable according to the actual state of things; for you, the states of being a soul and so forth, arising from ignorance and its associated attachments, are indeed false.
The apparent unity [of transmigrating beings] is contradicted by their very appearance, since we perceive them wandering in transmigration by the thousands. (YSi 147)
Until the complete eradication of saṃsāra, conventional transactions produced by that [mind] are perceived as uncontradicted,
being distinct from the occurrences of a dream.
Therefore, even the logical unity [of the self] is refuted by reasoning:
"Since their activities differ, it is inferred that other embodied beings, whose modes of existence are contrary [to one's own], cannot be denied, just as one's own self is. (YS 1.49)
Just as the inferences [of smoke] are distinct from the object of inference such as fire,
so too are they perceived through direct perception.
Likewise, how is it not distinct from other living beings?
If another cognizer were not inferred by means of specific activity,
then all worldly and Vedic practice would be abolished.
Nor can the cognition of the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower be based on a difference conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi);
for such a distinction would apply even to one's own body due to the differences between the head, hands, and so forth.
Just as there is a synthesis of unity when sensations arise in the head, hands, feet,
and so forth, so too should that [synthesis] be for you in all cases.
Due to the suffering of hell and the agony of childbirth, the enjoyments of previous births that occurred long ago have passed beyond the range of memory. (YS 3.18)
When pleasure, pain, and so forth arise simultaneously, the substrata [of these experiences] are clearly distinct;
how then could there be the delusion that they have a single object?

Nor can this worldly course of life be sustained even by numerous individual souls (jīvas), each of whom is imagined by their own specific ignorance and perceives only their own respective objects. (YS 156)
Those who are ignorant of future lives and perceive only their own respective dreams—
how could they establish that [teaching], which is bound solely by attachment and the like?
Furthermore, the self-luminosity, omnipresence, unity, and eternity that you yourself accept would contradict the non-duality of your consciousness. (YSsi 158)
Those factors are not consciousness itself, because even when consciousness is established,
disputes are observed regarding them.
And [the distinction between them] is due to the difference in their forms.
Nor are those [qualities] established through error, such that they would not contradict non-duality;
for those qualities are indeed established by the Vedānta texts which reveal reality.
Now, [if it is argued that] bliss, self-luminosity, eternity, greatness, and so forth,
are intended to be the very nature of Brahman itself—
then in that case as well, this must be analyzed.
Is that which is designated as "Brahman" merely those [qualities] such as pleasure and so forth? Or do they belong to it? Or rather, are they themselves what is designated by the name "Brahman"?
In the first case, the mention of those respective terms would be useless in both the Veda and the world;

furthermore, according to the previously stated reasoning, there would be duality [between Brahman and the world], yet [the scripture teaches] that [Brahman] is the cause of the birth and so forth of the universe. (YS 1.163)
For indeed, once Brahman has been accepted as the subject, the disputes among those speakers arise;
in that second case, by those very same disputants, Brahman itself becomes possessed of a second. (YS 164)
In the third [view], Brahman would be subject to division at every step because it consists of those [parts];
or else, Brahman would be a collection of them, like a forest consisting of a multitude of trees. (YS 165)
Excellence and manifestation are indeed distinct properties residing in the sun;
therefore, there is no example anywhere where the meaning of a sentence constitutes a division [of its own parts]. (YSi 166)

If words such as "knowledge" and "bliss" function in reference to one and the same reality by means of the exclusion of dullness, suffering, and so forth, then that which exists does not possess a second entity.
Are exclusions (apoha) non-existent, or do they exist, or are they neither?
If existence were real, it would have a second, consisting of the nature of the insentient and so forth, or else [it would be] otherwise.
The assertion that [Brahman] is distinct from both existence and non-existence has already been refuted;
and if that were the case, Brahman would not differ from jars and other such things.
Furthermore, if it does not impart a meaning contrary to its own non-insentience and other qualities,
then that [quality] cannot be excluded at all, just as in the case of words that share the same referent.

"But when the counter-positive is perceptible, that cognition which consists merely of another positive entity is itself non-existence; thus, even here, according to the wise, there is a coexistence with existence. (YSsi 171)

From what is it determined that the various distinctions between primary elements (bhūta) and their derivatives (bhautika) are distinct from both existence and non-existence— is it from perception and other means of knowledge, or rather from scripture?
Perceptual and other means of valid cognition arise as they sever their respective objects according to their nature, as far as is witnessed by themselves.
Just as when a blue object stands before one, there is no discussion of other colors;
the cognition has a single form, for by that [cognition] there is no perception of a white crystal.
Just as one who perceives sweetness in milk does not have the perception of the bitterness of neem,
so too all worldly and Vedic conventions are fixed. (YS 1.75)
If it is argued that "truth" is cognition, and that its basis does not exist when [the object] is unreal—that is not so.
If that [cognition] exists, then its basis must be postulated by virtue of its being an effect.
The sense organs, the marks [of gender], and so forth are also [merely] imagined, because they conform to its existence;
for neither simultaneity nor succession is possible regarding its delimitation or its production. (YS 1.177)

And as for the delusion that difference is not perceived because of the absence of conjunction with unity—that arises from the non-apprehension of the distinction between difference and mutual non-existence. (YS 1.178)
The very nature of entities, as fully grasped by perception,
would be the cause for the linguistic usage of difference, depending upon its counter-correlate.
Just as the cognition of "mere-that" establishes various verbal expressions such as "is not," or just as distinctions of shortness and length exist in a single six-finger span. (YS 180)
Thus, because the manifold world (*prapañca*) possesses many established forms and modes, its existence cannot be denied. (YS 1.81)
Scripture is not a means of valid cognition regarding such a matter because it culminates in action;
even if it were authoritative, it would not convey [the meaning] because its constituent words lack syntactic compatibility. (YSi 182)

If it is argued that the world is not "existent" because it is not perceived as such, and not "non-existent" because of sublation, then why is it not "existent" simply because it is perceived? And why is it not "non-existent" because of sublation? For what reason is the world neither?
Therefore, this ignorance has been resorted to by you through ignorance alone.
Furthermore, the property of the proliferation of difference is characterized by falsity;
it is either false or ultimate reality. Of these, the first alternative is not correct. (YS 184)
If that [duality] were false, the reality of the phenomenal world would be difficult to deny;
even if it were ultimately real, your non-dualism would be destroyed by that very fact.
All means of valid cognition appear to us as delineating their respective objects, as previously described,
by excluding them from non-existent things and from other objects.
For instance, when the cognition arises here that "the jar exists," at that time it does not admit either the non-existence of that jar or its being a cloth.
Now, as for what was said— that "it exists"— does that refer merely to the pot itself,
or to something else?
If it refers merely to that [pot], it follows that there is only the reality of Being (sadadvaita).
If it were established as a different entity, then it would be proven to be distinct from both existence and non-existence.
If it is thus held that "Brahman exists" based on the Upanishads, then for you, Brahman would fall into the state of being indefinable in terms of existence or non-existence, like a pot.
By means of the Vedic descriptions of bliss, truth, knowledge, and so forth, you yourself have thus established that Brahman is not of such a nature [as it appears]. (YS 190)
Furthermore, the assertion that the phenomenal world is distinct from both existence and non-existence would be abandoned;
for whatever is said to be of a certain nature, everything would necessarily become exactly like that.

Therefore, the cognition "it exists" arising with respect to jars and other objects brings about the realization of the ultimate reality of the specific configuration of each respective entity. (YS 192)

The existence of entities, established through their own respective fixed forms based on the exclusion of similar and dissimilar things—that is "Being" (sattā), and it is neither independent nor something else; how, then, can there be a discourse on non-duality (advaita) regarding that? (YSi 193)
Nor can the perception of various forms be denied; for it has already been stated previously that the object of cognition cannot possess the nature of consciousness itself. (YS Si 194)
Has something been established by you regarding consciousness, or not?
If it exists, there would be partiality; if it does not, your labor is in vain. (YS 195)
Therefore, cognitions whose internal distinctions are clearly perceived by their own inherent nature do not attain identity with external objects such as jars, which remain as they are.
The rule of simultaneous apprehension does not indeed apply to each individual cognition;
for if it did not exist, nothing could be an object of cognition, including that which possesses universals.
Because of the necessity of their simultaneous apprehension, the object cannot be other than consciousness;
for that which is independent of anything else in its own self-manifestation is precisely what the elders declare by the term "self-luminosity. (YSŚi 198)

When a certain object does not appear even while something else is appearing, that [object] is not a different entity from the latter, just as a false moon is not different from the real moon. (YSi 199)
If consciousness were non-manifesting, there would be no manifestation of the self or its objects;
thus, the world of manifold proliferation clearly follows as a transformation of consciousness.
(Do not thus despise external objects.)
Since their distinction is being protected by the more powerful direct perception (pratyakṣa), they do not follow inference (anumāna).
For in this way, "this," "I," and "I know"—these three clearly manifest directly as distinct from one another; this is witnessed by the self of everyone.
Furthermore, inference does not operate as a counter-argument to direct perception;
for instance, the non-hotness of fire is not inferred from its being a substance.
Moreover, this reason is contradictory, because the coexistence of two things is [the point at issue];
for even according to you, consciousness does not manifest together with itself.
A continuum of pure consciousness, free from the disturbances of blue and other [sensory objects],
shines forth during sleep and similar states;
however, an object does not exist in this way as something separate from its cognition.
Therefore, consciousness is real, whereas the object that is not perceived is non-existent.
This is the prattle of one who has not reflected upon the contradiction posed by his own words; for if this were so, the rule of simultaneous perception would be lost.
Since that which appears apart from something else also appears even without it—
just as a pot shines forth by itself even without a cloth. (YSi 207)
